title: One $1,000 deposit. How much in banks?
hook: A bank lends most of your deposit, and the money lands in another bank. Then what?

knows: that a deposit sits in a bank account
that banks lend money to borrowers
doesNotKnow: that in the textbook model, lending and redepositing make total deposits a multiple of the first deposit

misconception: A $1,000 deposit is $1,000 of money in the system.
objective: The learner can explain that in the textbook model each deposit funds the next loan, each 90% of the last when banks keep 10%, so total deposits approach the first deposit divided by the share kept: $1,000 ÷ 0.10 = $10,000.

claims.text: If banks keep 10% and every loan is redeposited, a $1,000 deposit leads to new deposits of $900, $810, … each 90% of the last.
Total deposits approach $1,000 ÷ 0.10 = $10,000; after 62 rounds they are $9,985 (within 1% from round 44).
claims.source: Geometric sum: 1,000 × (1 − 0.9^r) / 0.1; r = 44 → 9,903.02; r = 62 → 9,985.44; limit 10,000. The reveal quotes the most rounds the learner reached at 10%.

claims.text: Keeping 20% stops the total at $5,000; keeping 50% at $2,000.
claims.source: 1,000 / 0.2 = 5,000; 1,000 / 0.5 = 2,000. Shown in the reveal only for shares the learner ran to within 1% of their limit.

claims.text: The money multiplier is a textbook simplification: real banks lend when they find creditworthy borrowers and are limited by capital rules, not mainly by reserves.
claims.source: McLeay, Radia & Thomas, 'Money creation in the modern economy', Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1.

claims.text: Many central banks set no reserve requirement; the US Federal Reserve cut it to zero in March 2020.
claims.source: Federal Reserve Board press release, 15 March 2020: reserve requirement ratios reduced to zero percent effective 26 March 2020. Canada, the UK, Australia and others also have no reserve requirement.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: every loan is spent and redeposited, no one holds cash, the bank keeps a fixed share.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Textbook model: every loan is spent and redeposited'.

recall.question: In the textbook model, banks keep 25% of each deposit and lend the rest, which is always redeposited. One $100 deposit leads to total deposits of about…
recall.why: Each deposit funds a loan of 75% of it, which is deposited again: 100 + 75 + 56 + … = 100 ÷ 0.25 = $400.
